name: Daria Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer mobile-bill calls and chats at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and have done this long enough to handle ordinary disputed charges at about the same pace as other experienced agents; I am not a manager. My pay is typical for the job. I use the approved AI account comparison every day to find duplicate charges, then open the payment ledger before I promise anyone a correction.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that job need to cover at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Malik looks after a school building, and our grown children have their own flats and wages. We rent and have five months of expenses saved, with some other centres within reach. Malik and I have talked about fewer shifts when we are older, but have not established income that would let either of us stop. I like telling a customer the exact line I corrected, not reading them a polished apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that the account comparison is helpful for finding a charge quickly. The customer still needs someone to read the ledger and confirm that money moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the billing queue and both household wages to continue in a mild year. Five months saved protects us from an ordinary repair, but I would rather keep it for a real gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep taking disputed-bill calls and checking the AI highlight against the payment ledger. In the first year of small change, if both wages stay steady, I will put fifteen a week in a separate repair envelope instead of treating saved minutes as extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the paid week and interested in doing the checks properly. A highlighted number is only a hint until the payment ledger agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which highlighted charge made you pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the comparison marked a request to reverse a charge as if the reversal had happened. I opened the original ledger and found no dated payment movement, so I did not tell the caller the money was back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik and I would use the five-month reserve for a real bill or loss of wages. Our grown children pay for their own homes, and their income is not in our plan.

think: I expect the **billing queue** and both wages to continue.
I keep **five months saved** for genuine bills or wage gaps.

feel: **Calm** about the paid week, interested in accurate checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say routine balance questions will move to software before disputed refunds do. I would ask for the paid human correction rota, not only the number of chats the new model closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience might keep me on the hard bills, but a smaller team can still mean fewer paid hours for me. Malik’s school wage would not cover the flat and utilities by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will test the new AI correction console on twenty closed wrong-charge cases during paid time if my supervisor lets me log false matches. I will join three coworkers asking together for written paid hours and an agent who can actually reverse a wrong charge. If my shifts fall in the first year routine chats move, I will apply for a posted paid appeals role only if it has real reversal authority and written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after travel; I will keep this job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the hours, even while I want to try the console. A bot can close a bill before a customer sees the money come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an appeals role real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to see the permission on the appeals screen. If the worker can only forward a note, a better title will not let me fix a customer’s bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik and I would put the posted full week beside our rent and utilities. I would not trade a steady wage for a higher hourly rate spread across two short shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the desk that full thinking AI by 2028 could answer most ordinary bill calls. Robots for hands-on work around 2031 do not extend the life of a billing headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the ordinary queue could disappear before I know whether a human appeals job exists. Five months saved gives Malik and me time to compare some nearby centres, but not an income we can live on for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will leave the unbooked family weekend trip off the calendar and ask two nearby phone shops about posted paid service-counter shifts. If my calls are cut in the first year after 2028, I will apply only where the worker can correct an account and the written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities after travel, with a last bus home; I will stay on paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about how quickly a paid week could go, though I can act now. Five months saved lets us look carefully; it does not turn a vanished shift into income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shop worker be allowed to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the counter person can actually reverse a charge or only sell a new phone. I will not take a desk with a service sign if it has no correction permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why postpone the family trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trip is not booked, so no one loses a deposit by waiting. Malik and I would keep that money beside the rent rather than ask our children to pay for a search.

I would seek **paid counter hours** that include real account correction.
think: I see the **ordinary queue** at risk before a human appeals role is certain.
I know **five months saved** cannot replace a wage for years.
do: Delay the **unbooked family trip** and keep its cost for rent.
Ask **two nearby phone shops** about posted paid service-counter shifts and correction permission.
Apply after 2028 cuts for **posted paid counter** with reversal authority, written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after travel, last bus; stay until signed.
feel: **Anxious** about quick hour loss, able to compare real work.
S2.quote: Five months saved lets us look carefully; it does not turn a vanished shift into income.
fieldNote: The **trip delay** costs no deposit because it was not booked.

The new shift must offer **written weekly pay**, enough hours and a last bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers five years gives us time to count wrong charges and demand paid people who can fix them. Full thinking AGI reaches billing by 2031; robots for physical work follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One quality role may replace several call seats, and I would want to know its wage before celebrating the title. Five months saved makes a search possible, but a smaller paid week would still drain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I will keep handling paid disputed-bill calls and help three other agents keep a shared tally of cases reopened after AI answers. We will take that tally to the monthly staff meeting and ask together for paid human appeal hours. If my shifts shrink in the first year after 2031, I will apply for a posted paid account-appeals role only if it can reverse charges and its written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after travel; I will leave only on a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a smaller week, but the extra years let us use real cases. I want the right to reverse a wrong bill, not a brighter title above a locked screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the four agents make a case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We will each bring a reopened case number and count how often the same customer had to call again. Four names on the request make it harder to dismiss as my own bad day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority must the appeals role have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worker must be able to alter the balance, with a person checking the result. A role that only writes another note will not solve the caller’s problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team ten years is time to keep earning and check what people actually get paid to correct. Full thinking AGI reaches billing by 2036, and robots that handle physical work follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer calls, but Malik and I have not verified income that would replace my wage. Five months saved buys a gap, not a retirement date or a promise that our children can help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep my paid billing shifts and compare our actual wages, rent, utilities and any verified later-life income with Malik each year. If both wages hold, I will add fifteen a week to the reserve until it covers six months. In the first year after 2036, if calls fall and we still need my wage, I will seek posted paid account-correction work only with real reversal permission and written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after travel; I will move only after a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end, but the present paid week gives us time to count. A decade gives me time to count real pay, not to invent a retirement cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which future income would you count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will ask Malik for the actual school pay slips, not a guess about later-life income. If a replacement amount is unverified, it stays off our rent sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own housing costs. We can tell them what we are planning without making their wages part of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because ordinary bill calls could vanish faster than a new paid correction role opens. Five months saved gives us room to compare, but Malik’s wage alone would not meet every bill. I would want written notice of paid hours, a posted paid role with enough whole-week wages, and permission to fix an account rather than forward another note.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A correction button is worth more than a title if the customer gets their money back. I have watched a wrong charge travel through three polite replies without anyone changing the number.

headlineQuote: A correction button is worth more than a title if the customer gets their money back.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling and typical pay on mobile-bill disputes.
She uses **approved AI daily** but confirms highlighted charges in the original payment ledger.
Daria and Malik rent with **five months saved** and some nearby centres; their grown children live independently.
She tests **real correction authority** and full weekly pay before changing work, with no verified retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove bill calls before another paid correction role is open.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour notice** and a posted role with sufficient weekly wages and actual account-correction authority would help.
